items.q: The Corpus Hermeticum is best described as
choices: a set of Greco-Egyptian philosophical dialogues from late antiquity
a medieval grimoire of spirit conjuration
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the Hermetic treatises are products of the 2nd-3rd century CE Greco-Egyptian milieu, written as dialogues (Hermes to Tat, to Asclepius).

items.q: The Nag Hammadi library was uncovered in
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: thirteen codices found near Nag Hammadi in December 1945; they illuminate the same late-antique religious world as the Hermetica.

items.q: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the order's founding documents date to 1888 (London); its papers survive in archives and published collections.

items.q: In this academy's epistemic tiers, DOCUMENTED means a claim is
choices: supported by primary sources and scholarship
items.explain: The tier system: DOCUMENTED = archivally/scholarly evidenced; TRADITIONAL = transmitted within lineages; CONTESTED = disputed or unevidenced.

items.q: Aleister Crowley is most associated with
choices: the founding of the Golden Dawn
Thelema and the Book of the Law
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: Crowley proclaimed Thelema after the 1904 Cairo working that produced Liber AL vel Legis; the dictation claim is the historical datum.

items.q: Gerald Gardner is regarded as the founder of
choices: the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: Gardner's 1950s books and coven work founded modern Wicca; claims of older lineage are tiered separately.

items.q: Austin Osman Spare is best known in this curriculum for
choices: the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: Spare's atavistic art and sigil methods (The Book of Pleasure, 1913) became a core technique-line into chaos magic.

items.q: Late-antique Alexandria matters to this path because it was
choices: the headquarters of the Golden Dawn
the city Crowley lived in longest
the milieu where Hermetic, Gnostic, and Neoplatonic texts circulated
the site of the first Wiccan coven
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: Alexandria's philosophical schools are the documented context for the Hermetic and related corpora.

items.q: Which statement about the Corpus Hermeticum's dating is DOCUMENTED?
choices: Hermes Trismegistus was a single historical author of all seventeen treatises
The treatises are products of the 2nd-3rd century CE Greco-Egyptian milieu
The texts were dictated verbatim by the god Thoth
They were composed in 1888 by the Golden Dawn's founders
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: philology places the Greek treatises in the 2nd-3rd centuries CE; single-authorship and divine dictation are not evidenced claims.

items.q: The Golden Dawn's grade system counts as DOCUMENTED because
choices: its papers survive in archives and published collections
items.explain: DOCUMENTED tier = archivally evidenced. The order's rituals and grade papers are in the historical record regardless of what anyone feels.

items.q: Gardner's claim of an unbroken pre-Christian witch-cult lineage is tiered CONTESTED because
choices: historians find no evidence of continuity; it is a 20th-century construction using older materials
Gardner himself retracted it in print
items.explain: CONTESTED: the Murray thesis collapsed under scholarly scrutiny; modern Wicca's documented origin is Gardner's 1950s work.

items.q: The Asclepius differs from most of the Corpus Hermeticum in that it
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the Greek original is largely lost; the work survives mainly in the Latin Asclepius (with a Coptic fragment at Nag Hammadi).

items.q: This path treats the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram as
choices: a study object: a documented Golden Dawn practice, with no efficacy claim made
items.explain: Method: the ritual is studied as historical fact (DOCUMENTED practice); the path makes no claim about what it does.

items.q: The Book of the Law (1904) is DOCUMENTED as
choices: a text Crowley claimed was dictated to him; the dictation claim is the historical datum
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the manuscript, the Cairo working, and Crowley's claim are in the record; the claim's truth is not adjudicated here.

items.q: Chaos magic's 'paradigm shifting' (Peter Carroll) means
choices: the deliberate instrumental adoption of belief systems as tools
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: Liber Null (1978) frames belief as an instrument; the practitioner adopts and discards paradigms tactically.

items.q: The Principia Discordia (1963/1965) is
choices: a documented primary text of Discordianism, authored by Malaclypse the Younger and Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the authorship (Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley) and 1960s publication are in the record.

items.q: Which of these is a TRADITIONAL-tier claim?
choices: A fact with surviving manuscript evidence
A statistical finding from a survey
A lineage transmitted within an initiatory order, asserted by practitioners but not archivally proven
items.explain: TRADITIONAL = transmitted within a lineage; the claim of continuity is the practitioners', and the archive neither confirms nor refutes it.

items.q: The Nag Hammadi codices matter to Hermetic study because they
choices: illuminate the religious milieu of late-antique Egypt alongside the Hermetica
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: the codices (Gnostic, Hermetic-adjacent, philosophical) map the world the Hermetic writers inhabited.

items.q: 'As above, so below' is DOCUMENTED as
choices: a direct quote from the Greek Corpus Hermeticum
a phrase from the Latin Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet) tradition, widely cited in later alchemy
a line from the Wiccan Rede
items.explain: DOCUMENTED: 'Quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius' comes from the Latin Emerald Tablet; its Greek original is lost.

items.q: A student who can keep DOCUMENTED / TRADITIONAL / CONTESTED apart has mastered
choices: the path's core skill: epistemic sorting of esoteric claims
items.explain: The gate tests the single transferable skill of the path: sorting every claim into its honest tier.

lessons.title: The four quantities
body: Every DC circuit is described by four quantities. Current (I), measured in amperes, is the flow of electric charge — how many electrons pass a point per second. Voltage (V), measured in volts, is the electrical pressure pushing that charge, the potential difference between two points.

Resistance (R), measured in ohms, is the opposition to current flow. Power (P), measured in watts, is the rate at which electrical energy is converted into work, light, or heat. If current is water flow and voltage is water pressure, resistance is a narrow section of pipe and power is the work the waterwheel does.
Memorize the symbols and units cold: I = amperes (A), V = volts (V), R = ohms (Ω), P = watts (W). Every formula in this module is built from these four.

checks.q: A circuit has 2 A of current flowing at 12 V. Which quantity is the 'pressure' and which is the 'flow'?
checks.a: Voltage (12 V) is the pressure; current (2 A) is the flow.

checks.q: Name the unit for each: I, V, R, P.
checks.a: I: amperes, V: volts, R: ohms (Ω), P: watts.

lessons.title: Ohm's law
body: Ohm's law: V = I × R. Voltage equals current times resistance. Cover the quantity you want in the V-IR triangle and the remaining two show the formula: I = V / R, R = V / I.

The law only ever relates the voltage across, current through, and resistance of the same component. A common aptitude-test trap gives you the voltage across one resistor and the current through another — those do not combine.

worked.problem: 12 V is applied across a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current.
A 120 V circuit draws 0.5 A. Find the resistance.
24 V across 8 Ω. Find the current.

checks.q: 48 V across 12 Ω. Current?
2 A flows through 33 Ω. Voltage?
9 V across a resistor draws 0.3 A. Resistance?

lessons.title: Power
body: Power ties the other three together: P = V × I. Substituting Ohm's law gives two more forms: P = I² × R and P = V² / R. Use whichever form matches the quantities you know.

The I²R form is the reason overcurrent protection exists: double the current and the heat in a wire quadruples. Fuses and breakers are sized to interrupt current before I²R heating damages insulation.

worked.problem: 120 V × 2 A. Find the power.
A 100 W bulb runs at 120 V. Find its current and resistance.

checks.q: 12 V at 3 A. Power?
A 1500 W heater at 120 V. Current?
checks.a: I = 1500 / 120 = 12.5 A — which is why it needs a 20 A circuit, not a 15 A one.

lessons.title: Series circuits
body: In a series circuit there is one path, so the current is the same through every component. The source voltage divides across the components in proportion to their resistances, and the individual voltage drops always add back up to the source voltage — a useful self-check.
Total resistance is the simple sum: R_total = R1 + R2 + … A break anywhere opens the whole circuit, which is why series wiring is never used for building receptacles.

worked.problem: 12 V source, 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series. Find total current and each voltage drop.
worked.solution: R_total = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. I = 12 / 12 = 1 A everywhere. V_4Ω = 1 × 4 = 4 V; V_8Ω = 1 × 8 = 8 V. Check: 4 + 8 = 12 V ✓.

checks.q: 24 V with 6 Ω, 6 Ω, and 12 Ω in series. Current and drops?
checks.a: R = 24 Ω, I = 1 A. Drops: 6 V, 6 V, 12 V (sum 24 ✓).

lessons.title: Parallel circuits
body: In a parallel circuit every branch sees the full source voltage, so compute each branch current independently with Ohm's law and add them: I_total = I1 + I2 + … A break in one branch does not kill the others — this is how buildings are wired.
Equivalent resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … For two resistors the shortcut is R_total = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2). The equivalent is always smaller than the smallest branch resistor.

worked.problem: 12 V across 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel. Find branch currents, total current, equivalent resistance.

checks.q: 120 V across 60 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel. Currents and R_total?
checks.a: 2 A and 4 A; total 6 A; R_total = (60×30)/90 = 20 Ω. Check: 120/20 = 6 ✓.

lessons.title: Reading construction drawings
body: Three drawing types carry an installation: the plan (top view showing device locations), the one-line or riser diagram (the logical flow from service to panels to branch circuits), and elevations/details (how it mounts). Always start with the legend — every symbol on the plan is defined there.

Learn the core symbols: duplex receptacle (circle with two lines), single-pole switch (S), luminaire (circle with X or rectangle), panelboard (rectangle labeled 'P'). Schedules list exact catalog numbers; the plan shows where, the schedule shows what.

Practice drill: take any room plan and trace one branch circuit from the panel — through each device, noting what each symbol means — until you can narrate the whole run without looking at the legend.

checks.q: The plan shows a circle with two parallel lines in a bedroom. What is it, and where do you confirm?
checks.a: A duplex receptacle. Confirm the exact symbol meaning in the drawing legend, and the catalog number in the schedule.

lessons.title: Passage 1 — Lockout/tagout: the six steps (original practice text)
body: Before servicing equipment, the authorized employee identifies every energy source feeding the machine: electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, and gravity. Each source is isolated — breakers opened, valves closed, blocks set — and then locked with the employee's personal lock. Only the person who applied a lock may remove it.

After locking, the employee applies a tag naming themselves, the date, and the reason. Then comes the critical step most injuries skip: tryout. The employee attempts to start the equipment at its normal controls to verify isolation, then returns the controls to off. Stored energy is relieved last — capacitors discharged, springs released, pressure bled — and verified with a meter before hands touch conductors.

Question tiering: literal questions ask what the text states; inference questions ask what follows; vocabulary questions ask what a term means in context; application questions ask what to do in a new situation.

checks.q: (Literal) Who may remove a lock?
checks.a: Only the employee who applied it.

checks.q: (Inference) Why is tryout performed before relieving stored energy?
checks.a: Tryout verifies isolation using the machine's own controls; relieving stored energy comes after, so each hazard is handled in sequence.

checks.q: (Vocabulary) In context, 'relieved' most nearly means…
checks.a: Released or dissipated — capacitors discharged, pressure bled.

checks.q: (Application) A coworker asks to borrow your lock for 'just a minute.' Correct response?
checks.a: Refuse — locks are personal; only the applier removes them, and sharing breaks the chain of accountability.

lessons.title: Passage 2 — Reading a panel schedule (original practice text)
body: A panel schedule is the directory of a panelboard. Each row names a circuit number, the load it serves, the breaker size, the wire size, and the phase or pole. Odd numbers typically run down the left column, even numbers down the right, mirroring the physical breaker positions.

When troubleshooting, the schedule is read backwards from the symptom: a dead receptacle gives you a location, the location gives you a circuit number, the circuit number gives you a breaker — and the breaker size tells you what load the circuit was designed for. A 20 A breaker feeding fourteen receptacles is not automatically wrong, but it tells you where to look when it trips under load.
Never trust an unlabeled or outdated schedule. Verify with a meter: the schedule is a claim about the wiring, and claims get tested.

checks.q: (Literal) What five things does each schedule row name?
checks.a: Circuit number, load served, breaker size, wire size, phase/pole.

checks.q: (Inference) Why are odd numbers on the left and even on the right?
checks.a: To mirror the physical breaker layout, so a row maps directly to a breaker position.

lessons.title: Passage 3 — What a code excerpt is telling you (original practice text)
body: Code language is deliberately narrow. 'Shall' means mandatory; 'shall not' means prohibited; 'shall be permitted' means allowed but not required. An exception modifies only the section it sits under — it never grants a general waiver.

When a section lists conditions joined by 'and', every condition must hold. When joined by 'or', any one suffices. Fine print notes (FPNs) are explanatory only; they are not enforceable requirements, a favorite trap in code-literacy questions.
Read code excerpts the way the test reads them: identify the rule, identify who it applies to, identify the conditions, and check whether an exception narrows it.

checks.q: (Vocabulary) 'Shall be permitted' means…
checks.a: Allowed but not required.

checks.q: (Inference) An FPN says a method is 'recommended.' Is it enforceable?
checks.a: No — fine print notes are explanatory, not requirements.

checks.q: (Application) A section requires A and B, with an exception waiving B for dwellings. A dwelling has A but not B. Compliant?
checks.a: Yes — the exception removes the B condition for dwellings, and A holds.

body: Scenario 1: A journeyman repeatedly 'jokes' about an apprentice's accent in front of the crew. Model response: name it plainly and early — 'That's about his accent, not his work. Knock it off.' Scenario 3: You witness a coworker cornered by a vendor's comments and they laugh it off uncomfortably. Model response: check in privately afterward — 'That looked uncomfortable; want me to say something next time or walk with you?' Bystander responsibility means offering backup, not staging a confrontation on their behalf.

lessons.title: The apprentice-wage budget (worked example)
body: Build the budget from net pay, not gross. Example — illustrative figures only; substitute your training center's published wage scale: $19/hr × 40 hrs = $760/week gross, ≈ $2,900/month after taxes and deductions (estimate; your pay stub is the truth).

Fixed costs first: rent, transport, insurance, phone, minimum debt payments. Then variable: food, gas, household. Then pay-yourself-first: emergency fund target of one month's expenses before anything discretionary. Apprentice wages rise on a published schedule — map each raise to a specific debt or savings goal in advance, or lifestyle creep will eat it.

Credit scores move on five factors: payment history (largest), amounts owed/utilization, length of history, credit mix, and new inquiries. One 30-day late payment damages more than carrying a balance helps — autopay the minimums, then attack balances.

lessons.title: How the NEC is organized
body: The National Electrical Code is organized by chapters: Chapters 1–4 are general and apply to nearly everything; Chapters 5–7 cover special occupancies, special equipment, and special conditions; Chapter 8 covers communications systems; Chapter 9 holds the tables. Chapters 5–7 supplement or modify the general chapters — they never contradict them silently.

Inside a chapter, articles are numbered (e.g., Article 210, Branch Circuits), then parts, then sections (210.52). The two fastest tools are the table of contents (when you know the topic) and the index (when you know the keyword).

Two-minute lookup drill: pick a keyword — 'receptacle spacing', 'working space', 'conduit fill' — and time yourself finding the governing section. Under two minutes, repeatedly, is the skill. Never memorize article numbers from memory alone; always verify against the edition your authority having jurisdiction enforces.

checks.q: Which chapters are general, and which hold the tables?
checks.a: Chapters 1–4 general; Chapter 9 holds the tables.

lessons.title: Working space — Article 110
body: Article 110.26 requires clear working space in front of electrical equipment: at least 30 inches wide (or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater), 3 feet deep, and 6.5 feet of headroom. This space must stay clear — it is where a worker stands to operate equipment and where they retreat if something goes wrong.

Section 110.26(E) adds dedicated space: the area above a panelboard is reserved for the electrical installation — no foreign piping, ducts, or equipment may run through it. When you see storage piled in front of a panel on a jobsite, you are looking at a 110.26 violation.

checks.q: Minimum working-space dimensions in front of a panelboard?
checks.a: 30 in. wide, 3 ft deep, 6.5 ft headroom — 110.26.

lessons.title: Grounding concepts — Article 250
body: Two conductors are constantly confused. The grounded conductor (usually the neutral) normally carries current back to the source. The equipment grounding conductor (EGC, usually bare or green) normally carries no current at all — it is the dedicated fault path.

When a hot conductor faults to a metal enclosure, the EGC provides the low-impedance path that lets massive fault current flow, which is what trips the breaker and clears the fault. The grounding electrode system (rods, plates, water pipe) references the system to earth for lightning and surges — it does not clear faults; the EGC does.
Read Article 250 for the vocabulary first: grounded, grounding, grounded conductor, grounding conductor, bonding. Precision with these five terms prevents most grounding mistakes.

checks.q: Which conductor clears a ground fault, and how?
checks.a: The equipment grounding conductor — it carries fault current back to trip the overcurrent device.

lessons.title: Ampacity and conduit fill
body: Table 310.16 gives conductor ampacities: how much current a wire size may carry at a given insulation temperature rating. Continuous loads (on 3+ hours) must additionally be sized at 125% of the load — a 20 A continuous load needs conductors sized for 25 A.

Chapter 9 governs conduit fill: one conductor may fill 53% of the conduit's cross-section, two conductors 31%, and more than two only 40%. Use Table 4 for conduit areas and Table 5 for conductor areas, then divide.
Always confirm against the Code edition your local authority enforces — table values and derating rules change between editions.

worked.problem: Three 12 AWG THHN conductors in 3/4-inch EMT. Is the fill compliant?
worked.solution: Table 4: 3/4-in. EMT = 0.213 in². Table 5: 12 AWG THHN ≈ 0.0133 in² each → 3 × 0.0133 = 0.0399 in². Fill = 0.0399 / 0.213 = 18.7%. Three conductors → 40% limit. 18.7% < 40% ✓ compliant.

lessons.title: Rearranging formulas
body: Every electrical formula must be solvable for any variable. From V = I × R: divide both sides by I to get R = V / I; divide by R to get I = V / R. The operation that moves across the equals sign inverts: multiplication becomes division and vice versa.
From P = V × I: I = P / V and V = P / I. Combine them: given P and R, first find I = √(P / R), then V = I × R. Work one isolation at a time and check units at the end.

worked.problem: Solve P = I²R for I.
worked.solution: Divide by R: I² = P / R. Take the square root: I = √(P / R).

checks.q: Given V = 208 and P = 4500, find I.

lessons.title: Conduit offset math
body: An offset moves conduit around an obstruction using two equal bends. The distance between bend marks equals the offset depth times a multiplier set by the bend angle: 10° → 6.0, 22.5° → 2.6, 30° → 2.0, 45° → 1.4. Memorize these four.

The 30° offset is the workhorse: multiplier 2.0, so the marks are simply twice the depth apart. Shrink — the amount the conduit shortens — grows with angle, which is why small angles are preferred for long runs. Cosecant is the exact math (1/sin θ), but the multipliers are what the field uses.

worked.problem: A 6-inch offset at 30°. Distance between bend marks?
worked.solution: 6 × 2.0 = 12 inches between marks.

For number series, test patterns in order: constant difference, then multiplication/division, then alternating operations, then squares. Write the differences between consecutive terms — the pattern usually appears there.

For spatial reasoning (folding, rotation), eliminate answers that violate one visible feature before trying to build the whole shape mentally. Pace by the clock, not by perfection: a timed battery rewards every answered question, so never leave blanks and never spend three minutes on one item.

items.q:
Passage A (original). Voltage is the electrical pressure that pushes charge through a circuit, measured in volts. Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes. Resistance opposes that flow, measured in ohms. Ohm's law ties the three together: V = I x R, so current equals voltage divided by resistance. Resistors can be wired in series, end to end along a single path, or in parallel, across separate branches that share the same two connection points. In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances; this is why fuses and circuit breakers are wired in series with the load - every ampere of current must pass through the protective device. In a parallel circuit, each branch sees the full source voltage, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents; adding branches lowers the total resistance. A string of holiday lights wired in series all go dark when one bulb fails, because the single path is broken. Wired in parallel, each bulb keeps its own path, and each receives the full source voltage, so surviving bulbs burn at full brightness.

1. A 120-ohm resistor is connected across 24 volts. The current through it is ___.
According to Passage A, in a series circuit the total resistance is ___.
choices: the sum of the individual resistances
items.explain: Series resistances add; the passage states the total is the sum.

items.q: According to Passage A, which statement about parallel branches is true?
choices: Each branch carries the same current.
Each branch sees the full source voltage.
The total resistance is the sum of the branches.
A fuse must be wired in parallel.
items.explain: Parallel branches share the same two connection points, so each sees full source voltage.

items.q: According to Passage A, fuses are wired in series because ___.
choices: all current must pass through the protective device
items.explain: In series the same current flows through every component - the protective device sees every ampere.

items.q: According to Passage A, if identical bulbs are wired in parallel instead of series, each bulb is ___.
choices: dimmer, because the voltage is split
at full brightness, because each receives the full source voltage
off, because the path is broken
items.explain: The passage states each parallel bulb keeps its own path at full source voltage.

items.q: The main idea of Passage A is ___.
choices: fuses are more important than resistors
the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance, and how series and parallel wiring change circuit behavior
parallel circuits are always better than series circuits
items.explain: The passage defines V, I, R, states Ohm's law, then contrasts series and parallel wiring.

items.q:
Passage B (original). The National Electrical Code is not read like a novel. Electricians are taught to read code articles with the SQ3R method: Survey the article for headings and scope, turn each heading into a Question, Read to answer it, Recite the answer in your own words, and Review. This discipline matters because code language is precise in ways ordinary English is not. The word 'shall' means the rule is mandatory - it has the force of law wherever the Code is adopted. The phrase 'shall be permitted' means the action is allowed but not required; it grants permission and nothing more. Confusing the two changes compliance: treating a permitted method as required adds cost, while treating a requirement as optional creates a violation. One of the most-tested rules is the continuous-load rule: a branch-circuit conductor supplying a continuous load (three hours or more) must be rated at least 125% of the load. A 16-ampere continuous load therefore needs a conductor rated at least 20 amperes. SQ3R forces you to state that rule back before moving on - and to prove you know whether the Code says you 'shall' or 'shall be permitted' to use the next size up.

7. According to Passage B, the reading strategy recommended for code articles is ___.
choices: SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review
items.explain: The passage explicitly names SQ3R and defines each step.

items.q: According to Passage B, a continuous load of 16 amperes requires a branch-circuit conductor rated at least ___ amperes.
items.explain: The continuous-load rule: 125% of 16 A = 20 A.

items.q: According to Passage B, the word 'shall' in the Code means the rule is ___.
items.explain: 'Shall' carries the force of law wherever the Code is adopted.

items.q: According to Passage B, the phrase 'shall be permitted' means the action is ___.
items.explain: It grants permission and nothing more - allowed, never required.

items.q: According to Passage B, why must 'shall' be distinguished from 'shall be permitted'?
choices: Because the Code is written in Latin.
Because confusing a requirement with a permission changes code compliance - either adding cost or creating a violation.
Because the two phrases mean the same thing.
items.explain: Treating permission as requirement adds cost; treating requirement as optional creates a violation.

items.q: According to Passage B, the first S in SQ3R stands for ___.
items.explain: Survey: scan the article's headings and scope before reading in depth.

lessons.title: Circles, not squares
body: Circle packing is the problem of arranging circles inside a region so that no two overlap, usually as densely as the rules allow. It is one of the oldest problems in geometry — Kepler thought about sphere packing in 1611 — and one of the youngest in art, because only a computer can place ten thousand circles before lunch.

Generative artists reach for circles for three honest reasons. First, a circle looks the same from every direction: it has no corners to snag the eye, so a field of circles reads as texture rather than as a collection of objects. Second, circles nest against each other naturally; the gaps between them form their own secondary pattern, which is where much of the beauty lives. Third, a circle is the cheapest interesting shape to test — one distance check decides overlap — so packing algorithms stay simple enough to hold in your head.

You have seen packing everywhere without naming it: foam on a poured drink, the cells in a leaf photographed from above, pebbles sorted by a stream, the halftone dots of a printed photograph, stipple shading in an engraving. Each is a packing produced by some physical process. Generative art replaces the physical process with a procedure you design — and the procedure is the artwork as much as the image.

The piece that inspired this course, “7月16日” by Hitoshi Takagi on the creative-coding platform Pattlas, is a dense field of overlapping violet circles and loops. Its whole visual identity is carried not by drawn shapes but by eight parameters — Span, Factor, NC, Alpha, AngleX, AngleY, BLEND, and a text label. Learning to read that parameter block as a set of design decisions is the central skill of this course.

worked.problem: Why does a circle field look organic while a grid of circles looks mechanical, even when both use identical circles?
worked.solution: A grid repeats two spacings — horizontal and vertical — and the human visual system is a ruthless repetition detector. Packing breaks both spacings at once: every circle sits at a slightly different distance from its neighbors, so there is no period for the eye to lock onto. Randomness alone is not enough — pure random placement clumps and leaves voids — which is why packing algorithms exist: they produce irregularity with even coverage, the visual signature of natural processes.

checks.q: In your own words, what is the circle-packing problem?
checks.a: Arranging circles inside a region so none overlap, usually as densely as allowed — a geometric problem the course treats as a generative-art procedure.

checks.q: Name two natural and two designed examples of circle packing.
checks.a: Natural: foam bubbles, plant cells, pebbles. Designed: halftone print dots, stipple engraving, dot-matrix displays. Any two of each.

lessons.title: Rejection sampling: the honest algorithm
body: The simplest correct packing algorithm fits in a paragraph: propose a random position and radius, test the candidate circle against every circle placed so far, keep it if it overlaps nothing (with the required gap), otherwise throw it away and try again. Repeat until you have enough circles or you run out of patience. This is rejection sampling, and its honesty is its virtue — there is no hidden cleverness, so when the output looks wrong you know exactly where to look.

Two details make it practical. First, the random generator must be seeded: a seeded pseudo-random generator (the playground uses the mulberry32 algorithm) produces the same stream of numbers from the same seed, which means the same seed always grows the same field. Reproducibility turns accidents into studies — you can change one parameter and know the difference you see came from the parameter, not from a new roll of the dice.

Second, naive overlap testing compares each candidate against every placed circle, which is quadratic work — placing the thousandth circle costs a thousand distance checks, and most candidates get rejected late in the run when the field is crowded. The standard fix is a spatial grid: divide the canvas into cells roughly one diameter wide, file each placed circle under its cell, and test a candidate only against circles in nearby cells. The algorithm stays identical; only the bookkeeping gets faster.

Every packing run needs a stopping rule, because a truly dense field would reject candidates forever. Ours uses two: a target circle count scaled to the canvas area, and an attempts budget — a multiple of the target — after which we stop and keep what we placed. A run that stops on the budget instead of the target is telling you something: the parameters asked for more density than the geometry allows, and the honest response is a sparser field, not an infinite loop.

worked.problem: Trace four placements by hand. Canvas 100×100, gap 4, seeded so candidates arrive as: (20,20,r6), (26,20,r6), (60,60,r10), (63,63,r10). Which are accepted?
worked.solution: (20,20,r6) is first — accepted. (26,20,r6): distance to the first is 6, but the rule needs r1+r2+gap = 6+6+4 = 16 — rejected. (60,60,r10): far from everything — accepted. (63,63,r10): distance to (60,60) is about 4.2, needs 10+10+4 = 24 — rejected. Two accepted, two rejected: the rejections are the algorithm doing its job, not failing.

checks.q: Why must the random generator be seeded in a packing playground?
checks.a: So the same seed reproduces the same field — then a visible change can be attributed to the parameter you changed, not to a fresh random stream.

checks.q: What does a spatial grid change about rejection sampling — the result or the speed?
checks.a: Only the speed. The accepted set is identical; the grid just avoids testing candidates against circles that are too far away to overlap.

lessons.title: Faster cousins: Poisson-disc and front-chain
body: Rejection sampling is the algorithm you learn first because it is obviously correct. Two relatives dominate production use, and you should know what each buys you. Poisson-disc sampling (Robert Bridson's 2007 algorithm is the standard form) keeps an active list of placed points and proposes new candidates only in the ring around them, at a controlled distance. It guarantees a minimum spacing with far fewer rejections, and it produces the famously even 'blue noise' distributions used in rendering and stippling.

Front-chain packing takes a different tack: each new circle is placed tangent to two already-placed circles (and the boundary), walking a frontier around the packed region. It achieves very high density — the circles kiss — but the code is fiddlier and the result can look engineered rather than grown, because tangency chains leave characteristic curved seams.

The trade-off is always the same three-way pull: uniformity of coverage, density of packing, and simplicity of code. Rejection sampling is simple and honest but slow to densify. Poisson-disc is fast and even but enforces a minimum distance that fights the overlapping, loopy look of our inspiration piece. Front-chain is dense but intricate.

Our playground deliberately uses rejection sampling with a spatial grid: it is the easiest algorithm to reason about, it permits overlap control through the gap parameter (including the negative-gap looseness that lets circles kiss and overlap like the reference piece), and its failure mode — stopping on the attempts budget — is legible rather than mysterious. Learn the honest algorithm first; reach for the faster cousins when you can say exactly which trade you are making.

worked.problem: An artist wants the densest possible packing of identical circles for a print texture and does not care about code simplicity. Which method, and why?
worked.solution: Front-chain packing: placing each circle tangent to two existing circles achieves near-maximal density for equal circles, and the tangency seams read as intentional craft in a print. Poisson-disc would be the wrong choice here — its minimum-distance guarantee caps density below what tangency achieves.

checks.q: What does Poisson-disc sampling guarantee that plain rejection sampling does not?
checks.a: A minimum spacing between samples (even 'blue noise' coverage) with far fewer wasted candidates, via the active-list ring proposal.

checks.q: Why does this course's playground use rejection sampling instead of the faster methods?
checks.a: It is obviously correct and easy to reason about, its gap control permits the overlapping loopy look, and its stopping behavior is legible — the right teaching trade.

lessons.title: Span: the breathing room
body: Span sets the minimum gap the packer enforces between circles, on a 1–100 scale with a default of 28. Think of it as the field's breathing room. At low Span the circles crowd until they foam — edges kiss, gaps shrink to slivers, the field reads as a single continuous surface. At high Span each circle stands apart and the composition becomes a constellation: the negative space does half the talking.

Span also quietly controls quantity. A crowded field fits fewer large circles before the attempts budget runs out; a sparse field places its target count easily. In the playground the target count scales down as Span rises, which mirrors the real constraint: breathing room costs circles.

The useful discipline is to change Span alone, with a fixed seed, and watch the field reorganize. Same circles, same positions proposed — only the acceptance rule changes. That isolation is the whole method of this module: one axis at a time, seed fixed, eyes open.

worked.problem: With seed fixed, you raise Span from 28 to 70 and the field looks emptier but also calmer. Explain both effects.
worked.solution: Emptier: the larger enforced gap rejects more candidates, so fewer circles survive to the target — and the playground also lowers the target count. Calmer: wide even gaps remove the visual tension of near-touches; the eye stops hunting for collisions and reads the field as orderly. Same seed, so every surviving circle sits where it would have — Span only decided who survives.

checks.q: What happens to circle count as Span increases, and why?
checks.a: It falls: bigger enforced gaps reject more candidates, and the playground scales the target count down with Span.

checks.q: Why fix the seed when studying Span?
checks.a: To isolate the variable — with the seed fixed, differences in the output come only from the Span change, not from new random proposals.

lessons.title: Factor: how size falls off
body: Factor controls the size falloff across placement order, on a 0–100 scale defaulting to 15. The packer places large circles first and shrinks as it goes; Factor sets how steeply. At Factor 0 the decay is gentle — circles stay near their maximum size throughout, and the field feels monumental, almost architectural. At Factor 100 the radius collapses exponentially: a few giants, then a cascade of ever-smaller circles filling the interstices, the classic 'Soddy circles' cascade look.

This is a compositional lever disguised as a number. Large-to-small cascades create depth — the eye reads big circles as near and small ones as far, even on a flat canvas. Uniform sizes read as pattern; graded sizes read as space. The reference piece uses a mild Factor of 15: enough grading to feel grown rather than stamped, not so much that the small circles dissolve into noise.

Watch for the failure mode at extreme Factor: the tail of tiny circles can shrink below a pixel and contribute nothing but render cost. The playground clamps radius at a minimum so the tail stays visible as texture rather than vanishing.

worked.problem: You want a field that reads as deep space — a few near giants and a receding crowd. Which way do you push Factor, and what do you watch out for?
worked.solution: Push Factor up (toward 60–100) for the steep cascade. Watch the tail: if the smallest circles vanish, you have texture budget spent on invisible marks — either accept the clamp or lower Factor until the smallest visible circle still reads at your display size.

checks.q: What does Factor 0 produce, visually?
checks.a: Near-uniform circle sizes — a monumental, architectural field with little size grading.

checks.q: Why does size grading create a sense of depth?
checks.a: The eye interprets larger marks as nearer and smaller marks as farther, even on a flat surface.

lessons.title: NC and Alpha: building the violet field
body: NC sets the number of hue layers in the palette, from 1 to 99, defaulting to 3. With NC=3 the playground distributes circles across three violet-family hues — a blue-violet, a true violet, a magenta-violet — cycling by placement order. One layer is monochrome discipline; many layers approach a spectrum. The reference piece lives in violet, and three layers are enough to keep violet from going flat: the eye needs slight hue disagreement to perceive richness.

Alpha is opacity on a 0–255 scale, defaulting to 255 (fully opaque strokes). This is where the loops come from. Drop Alpha and overlapping strokes start to blend: intersections darken or glow depending on the blend mode, and the field gains the layered translucency of the reference piece. Alpha is the cheapest way to buy depth — no geometry changes, just ink behavior.

The two interact. High NC with low Alpha produces a watercolor wash of hues; low NC with full Alpha produces crisp graphic rings. The default — three hues, full opacity — is the bold poster look: every circle declares itself. Your studies should visit all four corners of this little square before settling anywhere.

worked.problem: Your field looks flat despite three hue layers. You may change one parameter. What do you try first and why?
worked.solution: Lower Alpha. Flatness here is a layering problem, not a hue problem: at full opacity every stroke occludes rather than blends, so overlaps read as edges instead of depth. Dropping Alpha lets intersections accumulate tone, which is what the eye reads as depth.

checks.q: What does NC control, and what is its default?
checks.a: The number of hue layers cycling through the palette; default 3, in the violet family.

checks.q: Why does lowering Alpha add depth without changing any geometry?
checks.a: Translucent strokes accumulate tone where they overlap, so intersections read as layering rather than occlusion.

lessons.title: AngleX, AngleY, and BLEND
body: AngleX and AngleY tilt the finished field, each on a −3.2 to 3.2 scale (roughly −π to π), defaulting to 1.1 and 1.2. After packing, every circle center is rotated about the canvas center by the average of the two angles. Small values produce a gentle drift — the field leans. Large values swing the composition dramatically and crop circles hard against the edges, which is a legitimate compositional device: the crop implies a field larger than the frame.

Two angles instead of one is a small generosity: their average sets the rotation while their difference is available as future expressiveness (in our mapping the average does the work; the pair is kept because the reference vocabulary has the pair). The lesson is about reading, not just using — parameter blocks often carry more joints than the current mapping exercises.

BLEND selects the canvas compositing mode. “blend” is the default source-over: new strokes cover old. “lighter” adds light — overlaps glow toward white, the neon look. “multiply” darkens intersections toward the ink color, the print look. “screen” is lighter's gentler cousin. Blend modes cost nothing to try and change everything about overlap: run the same seed through all four before you decide the piece is finished.

worked.problem: Same seed, same parameters, you switch BLEND from “blend” to “lighter” and the piece transforms from poster to neon sign. Explain.
worked.solution: Source-over occludes: each stroke covers what is beneath, so overlaps are just edges. Lighter adds pixel values: where strokes cross, light accumulates and intersections bloom toward white. The geometry never moved — only the arithmetic of overlap changed — which is why blend mode is the highest-leverage single parameter in the block.

checks.q: What do AngleX/AngleY do after packing, and what is the compositional effect of large values?
checks.a: They rotate the field about the canvas center; large values crop circles hard against the edges, implying a field larger than the frame.

checks.q: Contrast “lighter” and “multiply” on overlapping strokes.
checks.a: Lighter adds light — intersections glow toward white (neon). Multiply darkens — intersections deepen toward the ink (print).

modules.title: Reading Generative Work
modules.il_provides: The ethics and the craft of working from inspiration: honest attribution of the Pattlas piece, the line between inspired-by and copied, how to read any parameter block as a set of intentions, and a lab-notebook practice that turns tinkering into study.

lessons.title: Credit where it is due
body: This course exists because of a specific artwork: “7月16日” (“July 16th”) by Hitoshi Takagi, published on the creative-coding platform Pattlas. Its parameter block — TEXT “_circle”, Span 28, Factor 15, NC 3, Alpha 255, AngleX 1.1, AngleY 1.2, BLEND “blend” — is the vocabulary this course teaches you to read. That debt is recorded here, on the playground page, and in the course sources, because generative art is a community conversation and conversations name their speakers.

Here is the line we walked, stated plainly so you can walk it too. Inspired-by: taking the parameter vocabulary and the violet-field mood as a starting point, then writing our own packing algorithm, our own parameter mappings, and our own prose. Copied would have been: reproducing the artwork's image, reimplementing its exact renderer from decompiled source, or presenting its look as our invention. We did none of those things.

The rule generalizes: parameters and ideas are fair material; images and code are someone's work. When you publish studies made in the playground, credit the chain — the playground, this course, and Takagi's piece. Attribution costs nothing and buys you membership in the community you are learning from.

worked.problem: A student recreates the reference piece's exact look by screenshotting it and tracing the circles. They credit Takagi. Acceptable?
worked.solution: No. Credit does not cure reproduction: the image itself is the artist's work, and tracing it bypasses the entire generative procedure the course teaches. The honest path is to write a packer, tune parameters toward the mood, and credit the inspiration — process, not pixels.

checks.q: What did this course take from Takagi's piece, and what did it build itself?
checks.a: Taken: the parameter vocabulary and the violet-field mood, with attribution. Built: our own packing algorithm, our own parameter mappings, our own prose.

checks.q: Why doesn't credit alone make tracing the artwork acceptable?
checks.a: Because the image is the artist's work — credit cures omission, not reproduction. The generative path is to write your own procedure.

lessons.title: Parameters are intentions
body: Read a parameter block the way you would read an artist's statement. Defaults are the artist's voice: Span 28 says 'dense but breathing'; Factor 15 says 'graded, not cascading'; NC 3 says 'violet, but alive'; Alpha 255 says 'bold, every mark declares itself'; the tilt pair says 'the field leans, it is not axis-bound'. Eight numbers, and you already know the piece before it renders.

Ranges are the edges of the artist's curiosity: Span 1–100 admits both foam and constellation; angles spanning −π to π admit the full circle of tilts. A parameter the artist bothered to expose is a dimension they thought was worth playing — treat each exposed control as an invitation, and each fixed constant as a decision already made for you.

Your lab notebook practice: for every study, record seed, all eight parameters, and one sentence on what you were testing. After twenty studies you will own something no tutorial gives you — a personal map of the parameter space, with your taste marked on it.

checks.q: What do a parameter block's defaults tell you?
checks.a: The artist's voice — the default composition they consider the piece's home, readable as a set of design intentions.

checks.q: What should a lab notebook entry contain?
checks.a: Seed, all parameter values, and one sentence stating what was being tested.

lessons.title: Your first three studies
body: The course ends where studio courses should: with assignments, not summaries. Produce three studies in the playground, each varying primarily one axis, each with a notebook entry.

Study one, the foam: drive Span low (5–12), keep everything else near default. You are testing how dense the field gets before the attempts budget gives up — note where the rejections start winning. Study two, the constellation: Span high (60–85), Alpha down to ~140, BLEND on lighter. You are testing whether sparse marks with glowing intersections can carry a composition. Study three, the tilt: push AngleX and AngleY past 2.0 in opposite signs and watch the crop. You are testing the frame as a compositional tool.
Bring the three studies and their notebook entries to the gate assessment. The questions test whether you can predict what a parameter change will do — which is simply the notebook habit, examined.

checks.q: For the 'foam' study, which parameter moves and what are you observing?
checks.a: Span moves low (5–12); you observe density rising until the attempts budget starts winning and placements stall.
